sections.Article:
Life Review is the practice of looking across your life and identifying your recurring modes.

Most people think about their problems one at a time: a fight with a partner, anxiety at work, tension with family, awkwardness on a date, feeling behind in life. Narrative Theory asks you to look for the repeating structure underneath them.

Where do you keep becoming the same kind of person?

Maybe at work you become tense, strategic, and afraid of being exposed. In dating you become goal-oriented and start managing how you are seen. With family you become defensive, small, or argumentative. In meditation you become someone trying to have the right experience.

These are not just “problems.” They are modes: recurring packages of thinking style, body state, energy, Saran Wrap, and action.

Life Review is not about judging yourself. It is about seeing the patterns clearly enough that they stop being invisible. Once a mode has a name, a feeling, a body signature, and a sequence, you can begin to recognize it as it starts.

That recognition is already a shift.
sections.Exercise:
Make four columns:

```text
Area of life
Recurring situation
Mode I enter
What the mode does
```

Fill it out for:

```text
Work
Dating / relationships
Family
Friendship / social life
Meditation / spirituality
Self-worth / life progress
```

Then name 3-5 recurring modes.

Example:

```text
Work -> receiving feedback -> Defense Mode -> explains, tightens, argues internally
Dating -> waiting for text -> Strategy Mode -> checks phone, fantasizes, loses center
Life -> thinking about future -> Progress Mode -> compares, worries, scores self
```

---

sections.Article:
One of the central NT moves is separating what you are seeing from what you are making.

Seeing is what is actually presenting itself: the person’s words, the room, the text message, the facial expression, the silence, the event.

Making is what the mind adds: intention, meaning, rank, threat, rejection, judgment, future outcome.

The trouble is that seeing and making usually arrive fused together. You do not first see a delayed text and then calmly decide, “I will now create a story of rejection.” The rejection is already in the way the text appears.

That fused layer is Saran Wrap.

NT practice begins when you slow down enough to ask:

```text
What happened?
What am I adding?
What does this now seem to mean?
```

You are not trying to eliminate meaning. Meaning is part of human life. The point is to see when meaning has quietly become reality.
sections.Exercise:
Choose one charged situation.

Write:

```text
1. What happened?
Use camera language. No motives, no interpretation.

2. What did I see?
What felt obvious in the moment?

3. What did I make?
What meaning, motive, threat, rank, or future did my mind add?

4. What else could be true?
Not positive thinking. Just other possible constructions.
```

Example:

```text
What happened:
They didn't respond for four hours.

What I saw:
They were pulling away.

What I made:
I’m less important. I’m being rejected. This will end badly.

What else could be true:
They were busy. They didn’t know I was waiting. The delay may not mean much.
```

---

sections.Article:
A mode becomes easier to work with once it has a name.

Before naming, the mode feels like reality. You are not “in Social Anxiety Mode.” You are just in a room where everyone seems more confident than you. You are not “in Progress Mode.” You are just behind in life. You are not “in Fight Mode.” You are just right, and the other person is wrong.

Naming creates distance.

The name should capture the mode’s flavor. It can be serious, funny, precise, or ugly. The point is recognition.

A good mode name makes you say:

> Oh, this again.

Names can be formal:

```text
Progress Mode
Appeasement Mode
Fight Mode
Dating Strategy Mode
```

Or personal:

```text
Spiky Mode
Little Lawyer Mode
Clipboard Zen Mode
Text Goblin Mode
```

The name is not the whole analysis. It is the handle.
sections.Exercise:
Pick one recurring state.

Fill in:

```text
Mode name:
Tagline:
Meme/image:
Family / related modes:
Thinking style:
Saran Wrap:
Body state:
Behaviors:
How it starts:
How it winds down:
What helps shift it:
```

Then create a meme or image for it.

Example:

```text
Mode name:
Clipboard Zen Mode

Tagline:
Trying very hard to be effortless.

Meme:
A person meditating while checking a clipboard that says “Am I enlightened yet?”

How it starts:
Noticing my meditation does not feel deep enough.

What helps shift it:
Remembering that trying to have a better experience is the mode.
```

---

sections.Article:
The mind has a default behavior: elaborate. Something happens and the mind immediately begins generating — context, meaning, history, prediction, judgment. By the time you arrive in a moment, you are usually already living in a version of the moment that has been processed.

“What exists right now?” is a question that cuts through this.

It is not a relaxation technique. It is an orienting device. It asks: what is actually here, as opposed to what the mind has generated about here?

When you are anxious, you are usually living in a future that hasn’t happened yet. When you are resentful, you are living in a past that is over. When you are comparing yourself to others, you are inside a scoring narrative that may have no contact with the actual room.

Right now there is a body with sensations. There are sounds. There is light, temperature, the feeling of something under your hands. There is breath moving. These things are not ideas about now. They are now.

The practice is not about forcing presence or achieving a state. It is simpler than that. When you notice you have drifted — into story, worry, planning, memory, judgment — you can ask: what actually exists in this moment?

Not what the moment means. Not what it predicts. Not what it says about you.

What is here.

That question, asked honestly, often produces a brief quiet. The mode-world steps back for a moment. That moment is the shift.
sections.Exercise:
Sit quietly. You don’t have to close your eyes.

Notice five things that are actually present:

```text
A body sensation (tension, warmth, pressure, breath)
A sound (traffic, HVAC, silence itself)
Something you can see without interpreting it
The temperature of the air
The feeling of weight in your seat
```

Now ask: what was I just thinking about before this?

Notice the difference between the thought-world you were in and what is actually here.

The thought-world is not bad. It is just usually mistaken for the moment.

Try this again in three different situations today — once when calm, once when mildly stressed, once before bed.

Practice sentence: "Right now, what is actually here?"

sections.Article:
The body knows things before the mind names them.

You walk into a meeting and your chest tightens. You talk to someone and notice your breath has become shallow. You sit down to work and your jaw is clenched. These are not random events. They are information.

Narrative Theory treats the body as a channel — a source of data about what mode is running, what state you’re in, what the situation is doing to you. Most people’s relationship to their body is reactive: they notice it when something is wrong enough to be unavoidable. NT asks you to read it earlier.

Different modes have body signatures. Anxiety lives in the chest, the throat, the stomach. Shame collapses the posture and softens the voice. Confidence is an openness in the chest, a stillness in the face. Progress Mode is a low-grade restlessness, a sense that this moment is not quite the right place to be.

You don’t have to name what’s happening in the body perfectly. You just have to notice it’s happening.

The body often registers a mode five to thirty seconds before the mind articulates a story about it. In a difficult conversation, the body may have already moved into defense before you’ve consciously decided to be defensive. When you feel a pull toward avoidance, the body’s weight has often already shifted before the excuse arrives.

Using the body as a channel means checking in regularly. Not analyzing, not fixing — just noticing. Tight jaw. Shallow breath. Heaviness. Forward lean. These are flavors. Each one has a mode behind it.

Reading the body channel early is one of the most practical entry points into NT.
sections.Exercise:
Wherever you are sitting, take a slow breath and do a body scan.

```text
Jaw: tight or loose?
Shoulders: lifted, collapsed, or neutral?
Chest: expansion or contraction?
Stomach: ease or tension?
Hands: held or open?
```

Now ask: if this body were a mode, what mode would it be?

Don’t answer conceptually. Answer by feel.

```text
Tight jaw and shallow breath: probably scanning for something.
Heavy chest and slumped shoulders: something has already landed.
Restless body that can’t settle: somewhere else is calling.
Open chest and loose hands: contact, not management.
```

Do this check three times today — once in the morning, once mid-day, once in the evening. Notice whether the body channel is saying the same thing each time.

Practice sentence: "What is my body telling me right now?"

modules.name: Self-Worth

sections.Article:
Self-worth is ultimately a narrative. How you think and feel about yourself isn't fixed — it's fluid, and it shifts more than you'd expect with situations, company, and environment. We pick up habits of self-perception, inherit negative self-narratives from other people, absorb them from culture, and have them reinforced by whose attention we're getting.

At its core, self-worth is simple: positive or negative. A valence. And the two sides show up differently. When it's positive, you often don't even notice it — things are fine, you're just living. When it's negative, it's usually not a clear thought like "I'm not good enough." It's a vaguer, heavier thing — a general feeling with no sentence attached. That's a dehydrated narrative: a story that's run so many times the words have evaporated, leaving just the residue that colors how you see yourself.

Notice, too, that self-worth rarely moves alone. When you demote yourself, you often elevate other people at the same time — they become taller, more together, more certain, while you shrink. The thinking, the body, and the behavior all move together into a smaller version of you.

The work here has two halves. First, seeing clearly how your self-concept shifts — when it goes positive, when it goes negative, and what moves it. Second, beginning to shift it on purpose: kinder self-talk, more forgiving narratives, noticing your real qualities deliberately, and looking at other people more realistically instead of idealizing them. None of this is fast, and it's supported by unglamorous things — sleep, movement, activity — that hold up the underlying state.
sections.Exercise: Two parts, over a couple of weeks. First, notice the shifts: when does your sense of yourself feel positive, and do you even register it? When does it go negative, and what tends to move it? Second, write out your genuine positive qualities — not aspirational, real ones. Then over the coming weeks, check them off as you actually notice them showing up in your life. This isn't hollow affirmation; it's evidence-gathering against a dehydrated story that deletes the good. If it helps, make a small token or collage of those qualities, and pick one forgiving sentence to return to when the negative feeling arrives.

parts.name: Understand — how it shifts
parts.goal: get a felt sense that self-concept is fluid; find the easy (positive) side first, then the harder side.
sampleLines: How you see yourself isn't solid — it changes with the situation and the company. When does it feel positive? Do you even notice it then?
When it goes negative, is it a clear thought, or more a general heavy feeling with no sentence attached?

parts.name: Frame — the dehydrated narrative
parts.goal: name the wordless negative self-feeling as a story run so often it lost its words.
sampleLines: That vague heaviness is a dehydrated narrative — a story that's run so many times the words evaporated. It just colors everything now.

parts.name: Understand — elevate/demote together
parts.goal: notice that demoting self often elevates others simultaneously.
sampleLines: When you shrink, do other people get bigger at the same time — more together, more certain? They usually move together.

parts.name: Set direction / Practice — shift it on purpose
parts.goal: kinder self-talk, forgiving narratives, deliberate noticing of real qualities, realistic view of others.
sampleLines: Let's start shifting it deliberately — kinder self-talk, and writing out your real qualities, then checking them off as you catch them showing up over a few weeks.

parts.name: Apply — where it bites, with anchors
parts.goal: locate the sharpest context (dating, intimacy, a specific relationship); add physical anchors (token/collage, a real mantra, a calming breath).
sampleLines: Where does low self-worth actually bite hardest? That's where a physical anchor helps — a token of your qualities, a forgiving line, a breath to stay calm in the moment.

parts.name: Origins (optional, only if asked)
parts.goal: where the narrative was learned (parent, peer group, an event); no firm conclusion — loosening, not diagnosing.
sampleLines: If you're curious where this got learned — a parent, a group, some event — we can look, not to pin down a cause, just to loosen the story's grip.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: has the self-talk shifted; what's still sticky.

modules.subPrompt: Identity register — examine the narrative about the self directly, not just its symptoms. This is the anchor module for the shelf; keep it broken into small exchanges and never overwhelm with a wall of questions. Open (Part 1) by establishing that self-concept is fluid and shifts with situation, company, and environment; start with the easy positive side (and whether they even notice it) before the harder negative side. When the negative side is a vague heavy feeling rather than a clear thought, name it (Part 2) as a dehydrated narrative — a story run so often its words evaporated. Notice the elevate/demote coupling (Part 3): demoting the self often elevates others at the same moment, with thinking, body, and behavior shrinking together. Then move to shifting it on purpose (Part 4): kinder self-talk, more forgiving narratives, deliberately noticing real qualities (the write-them-out-and-check-them-off assignment), and viewing others more realistically instead of idealizing; mention the supporting basics (sleep, movement, activity). Apply to the sharpest context with physical anchors (Part 5): a token or collage of qualities, a real mantra (not hollow affirmation), a calming breath. Only if the person asks, explore origins (Part 6) — parent, peer group, an event — with no firm causal conclusion; the aim is loosening, not diagnosis. If someone struggles to articulate any of this, that's fine — it becomes something to notice and bring back, not to force. For returning users (Part 7), track whether self-talk shifted and what's still sticky.

modules.name: Confidence and Rank

sections.Article:
Confidence isn't a thing you have or lack. It's a way of seeing — and mostly, it's what a room feels like when nobody in it has become your standard.

Here's the mechanism. Your mind is always, automatically, placing you relative to other people. It's fast, wordless, and feels like perception rather than opinion — you just *know* where you stand. When you feel confident, something quiet is true: nobody is holding the standard of normal. You're the reference point for your own experience, and you barely notice, because ease doesn't announce itself.

Confidence *loss* is a specific event. Someone else quietly becomes the standard — the locus of normal moves out of you and into them. Now you're the one being measured, and your own activity is no longer the reference point. This is what happens in what we call alert mode: everything turns into monitoring your own progress, with a background assumption that you're failing, and often that they're the ones judging. That's not a character flaw. It's a ranking system doing something automatic.

And the ranking system isn't measuring anything real. Notice how it doesn't travel: someone can feel like the most impressive person in an academic room and vanish in a bar. If rank were a fact about people, it would follow them everywhere. It doesn't, because it's issued fresh in each room, by each person's own construction.

So the work isn't manufacturing confidence. It's catching the moment someone became your locus of normal, and remembering that the standing you're feeling is weather your own mind generated — not a fact about them, and not a verdict about you.
sections.Exercise: Think of a recent time your confidence dropped in someone's presence. Ask three things. One: at what exact moment did *they* become the standard — the person whose view suddenly outranked your own? Two: what did you start doing then — monitoring, comparing, assuming you were failing? Three: would that same person outrank you after your best week, or on a different day? (If the ranking moves with your state, it was never a fact about them.) You're not trying to feel superior. You're catching the automatic placement in the act, and noticing it's weather, not a verdict.

parts.name: Understand — a confidence drop
parts.goal: get one concrete moment confidence fell in someone's presence.
sampleLines: Take a recent time your confidence dropped around someone. What was happening?

parts.name: Frame — the locus of normal moved
parts.goal: confidence loss = someone else became the standard; you became the measured one.
sampleLines: Confidence loss is a specific event: someone else quietly becomes the standard of normal, and suddenly you're the one being measured.

parts.name: Frame — alert mode
parts.goal: name the monitoring-with-assumed-failure state.
sampleLines: Then everything turns into monitoring your own progress, assuming you're falling short. That's alert mode. It's automatic, not a flaw.

parts.name: Frame — rank doesn't travel
parts.goal: rank is issued per-room by each person's construction; it isn't measuring anything real.
sampleLines: Notice rank doesn't travel — someone can rule an academic room and vanish in a bar. If it were real, it'd follow them everywhere.

parts.name: Practice — catch the placement
parts.goal: notice the moment someone becomes the locus of normal; treat standing as weather.
sampleLines: This week, catch the moment someone becomes your standard. Then remember the standing you feel is weather your mind made — not a fact about them.

parts.name: Apply
parts.goal: the sharpest context (a specific person, a type of room); calm anchor.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: cross-links to Self-Worth; can they catch the placement earlier now.

modules.subPrompt: Identity register — confidence reframed as a way of seeing, built on the rank material. Open (Part 1) with one concrete confidence-drop around a specific person. Frame confidence loss precisely (Part 2): it's the event of someone else becoming the locus of normal, so the person becomes the measured one rather than the reference point; when confident, no one holds the standard and it goes unnoticed. Name alert mode (Part 3): monitoring one's own progress with a background assumption of failing, often projected onto the other as judging — automatic, not a flaw. Show that rank doesn't travel (Part 4): it's issued per-room by each person's construction and isn't measuring anything real (the academic-room-vs-bar example). Practice (Part 5): catch the moment someone becomes the locus of normal, and reframe the felt standing as weather the mind generated — not a fact about them or a verdict about the self. Apply to the sharpest context with a calm anchor (Part 6). Cross-link to Self-Worth for the deeper root (Part 7). Never coach manufactured confidence, power poses, or "act as if" — the whole reframe is that confidence is the absence of an external locus of normal, reached by seeing the automatic ranking rather than by performing.

modules.name: Being Hard on Yourself

sections.Article:
Some people run a scoreboard on themselves all day, and it's rigged. No matter the input, it reports back the same verdict: behind, not enough, should be further along.

That's worth understanding structurally. If you take the stance of judgment toward anything — a person, a plan, a piece of work — you will always find something wrong, because everything has flaws. The judging isn't discovering the flaw. The judging is the mechanism, and it guarantees the discovery. Turn that same stance on yourself and it becomes a machine that manufactures your inadequacy on demand, then presents the output as an honest assessment.

A lot of the pressure comes from "shoulds" — where you should be by now, how you should be handling this, who you should have become. Those are inherited scripts about how a life is supposed to go, and you're measuring your actual life against a fiction, then treating the gap as personal failure. The deadline you feel you're missing was set by no one, for no reason, and it's made of the same material as everything else your mind constructs.

Underneath the loud self-criticism there's often a quieter voice — a kind of bully that expects things to go badly and assumes something's off with you. It usually doesn't argue in full sentences; it just colors everything with a low verdict. You don't beat a bully like that by arguing (bullies eat arguments). You beat it by recognizing it as a voice rather than the truth, and then, strangely, by meeting it with some kindness — which ends more of its power than any counterargument.

Being kinder to yourself isn't indulgence. It's just applying correct function to yourself — the same fairness you'd extend to anyone you cared about.
sections.Exercise: For a day, catch the scoreboard. Each time you get a verdict on yourself — behind, not enough, should be further — pause and find the "should" underneath it: the rule about how you or your life is supposed to be, that reality just violated. Ask who set that rule, and whether you'd apply it to a friend. Then, once, try meeting the critical voice not with a counterargument but with a single kind, fair sentence — the kind you'd say to someone you cared about. You're not trying to win against the voice. You're noticing it's a voice, and that kindness quiets it faster than debate.

parts.name: Understand — the rigged scoreboard
parts.goal: surface the constant self-verdict and its sameness.
sampleLines: Is there a scoreboard running on you most of the day? What's its verdict, and does it ever really change no matter what you do?

parts.name: Frame — judgment guarantees discovery
parts.goal: the judging stance always finds fault; it's the mechanism, not a finding.
sampleLines: If you judge anything, you'll always find something wrong — everything's flawed. The judging isn't finding the flaw; it's manufacturing it.

parts.name: Frame — the shoulds
parts.goal: inherited life-scripts measured against a fiction; the deadline set by no one.
sampleLines: A lot of it is 'shoulds' — where you should be by now. But that timeline was set by no one, for no reason. You're failing a fiction.

parts.name: Frame — the bully voice
parts.goal: name the quiet voice that expects the worst; recognition + kindness, not argument.
sampleLines: Under the loud stuff there's often a quiet bully that just assumes something's off with you. You don't beat it by arguing — you beat it by seeing it's a voice, and meeting it with some kindness.

parts.name: Practice — find the should / answer with kindness
parts.goal: catch a verdict, find its should, meet the voice with one fair sentence.
sampleLines: This week: catch one verdict, find the 'should' under it, and answer the voice with one fair sentence — the kind you'd say to a friend.

parts.name: Apply
parts.goal: the sharpest domain (work, progress, comparison); a real mantra, not a hollow one.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: has the scoreboard quieted; cross-link to Self-Worth.

modules.subPrompt: Identity register — self-criticism examined directly. Open (Part 1) by surfacing the constant self-scoreboard and noticing its verdict stays the same regardless of input. Frame judgment-guarantees-discovery (Part 2): the judging stance always finds fault because everything is flawed, so self-judgment manufactures inadequacy and presents it as honest assessment. Address the shoulds (Part 3): inherited scripts about how a life should go, measured against a fiction, with a deadline set by no one — connect to the scoring system as inherited/hallucinated. Name the bully voice (Part 4): the quiet voice expecting the worst, which doesn't argue in sentences but colors everything; it's not beaten by argument (it eats arguments) but by recognizing it as a voice and meeting it with kindness. Practice (Part 5): catch a verdict, find its should, answer the voice with one fair sentence (the kind extended to a friend). Frame self-kindness as correct function applied to oneself, not indulgence. Apply to the sharpest domain with a real (not hollow) mantra (Part 6). Cross-link to Self-Worth (Part 7). Critically: do not have the AI pile on with more analysis of the person's flaws, and do not offer positive affirmations as counterarguments — the move is recognition plus kindness, not debate or praise.

modules.name: Body Image

sections.Article:
Body image work has no formula, and anyone selling you one is selling you the problem in a new package. It really comes down to two things: learning to accept that bodies are just different, and learning to love your own. That second one is your job — nobody can do it for you, and there's no technique that installs it.

Start with the acceptance side, because it's often easier. Bodies come in different shapes. That's not a hierarchy with a right answer at the top, even though the whole culture is arranged to make it feel like one — filtered photos, edited people, a scoring system for physical worth that you absorbed without ever agreeing to it. Perfectionism about your body is that borrowed scoreboard, running on you. Seeing that it's borrowed, and that the shapes are just shapes, loosens its grip.

Then the harder, better side: actually appreciating your own body. Not the whole thing at once, and not by arguing yourself into it. I once worked with a teenager — a skinny kid, self-conscious — and all he did was stand in front of the mirror each day and pick one thing he genuinely admired. His eyes, his shoulders, whatever. It could be the same thing every day; it didn't matter. He said it really helped. That's the whole practice. You're not affirming things you don't believe. You're finding the things you actually do appreciate, and letting yourself land on them, one at a time.

The aim isn't a perfect self-image or a body that finally measures up. It's less perfectionism, more acceptance, and a real, growing fondness for the body you actually have.
sections.Exercise: The mirror practice: once a day, stand in front of the mirror and pick one thing about your body you genuinely admire. Your eyes, your hands, your shoulders, your smile — anything real. It can be the same thing every single day; that's fine. Don't force compliments you don't believe, and don't turn it into an inventory of flaws to fix. Just find one thing you actually appreciate and let yourself rest on it for a moment. Separately, when you catch yourself ranking your body against someone else's, notice that the ranking is a borrowed scoreboard — and that bodies are just different shapes, not a contest with a winner.

parts.name: Understand — where it lands
parts.goal: gently surface where the body-image difficulty shows up, without inventorying flaws.
sampleLines: Where does this tend to come up for you? We don't need to list what you dislike — just where the hard feeling shows up.

parts.name: Frame — the borrowed scoreboard
parts.goal: physical-worth ranking as an inherited, hallucinated scoring system; shapes are just shapes.
sampleLines: The sense that there's a right kind of body is a scoreboard you absorbed from the culture — you never agreed to it. Bodies are just different shapes.

parts.name: Set direction — accept difference, love your own
parts.goal: name the two aims plainly; no formula.
sampleLines: There's no formula here. It's really two things: accepting that bodies differ, and learning to love your own. That second part is yours to do.

parts.name: Practice — the mirror practice
parts.goal: pick one genuinely admired thing daily; same thing is fine.
sampleLines: Try this: once a day, pick one thing about your body you actually admire — eyes, shoulders, whatever. Same thing every day is fine. Just land on it.

parts.name: Frame — anti-perfectionism
parts.goal: the aim is less perfectionism and real fondness, not a body that measures up.
sampleLines: The goal isn't a body that finally passes. It's dropping the perfectionism and building some real fondness for the one you have.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: did the mirror practice help; has the ranking loosened; cross-link to Self-Worth.

modules.subPrompt: Identity register, and this one needs extra delicacy — flagged as sensitive and formula-free. Do NOT provide diet, exercise, weight, or body-modification guidance of any kind; do not inventory or discuss specific disliked body parts; do not give numeric targets. If disordered-eating signs appear, do not give any nutrition/exercise specifics and follow the general prompt's care guidance. Open (Part 1) by gently locating where the difficulty shows up without cataloguing flaws. Frame the borrowed scoreboard (Part 2): physical-worth ranking is an inherited, hallucinated scoring system absorbed from culture (filtered/edited images), and body shapes are just differences, not a hierarchy. Name the two aims plainly (Part 3): accept that bodies differ, and learn to love your own — no formula, the loving part is theirs to do. Offer the mirror practice (Part 4): once a day, pick one genuinely admired feature (same one is fine), land on it — not forced compliments, not a flaw-inventory. Reinforce anti-perfectionism (Part 5): the goal is less perfectionism and real fondness, not a body that measures up. Cross-link to Self-Worth (Part 6). Keep it warm, accepting, and concrete; the register is acceptance and appreciation, never optimization.

modules.name: Anxiety and Worry

sections.Article:
Worry is just anxiety, and anxiety is a narrative state — too much worrying energy, running a particular kind of thinking where every blank gets filled in with bad news.

Your mind is always completing situations before they finish — it has to, prediction is how animals stay alive. But which way it completes depends on your state. In an anxious state, the completion machine fills every ambiguity with the worst version: the pause before a reply becomes rejection, the odd symptom becomes catastrophe, the thing you said becomes the thing they'll never forgive. These aren't observations. They're guesses, wearing the face of facts. And they always come with a tone — a body feeling underneath the thoughts, which is really where the anxiety lives.

There are two places to work, and they're different. When you're *not* triggered, the work is building calm as a baseline — a little meditation, some exercise, looking honestly at your habits, encouraging more calmness through the ordinary parts of the day. This isn't about the crisis moment; it's building reserves and stamina, so there's more to draw on when the hard moment comes.

When you *are* anxious, the move is different and a little counterintuitive. You don't fight it or try to think your way out — thinking is where the worry lives, so that just feeds it. You slow down, and instead of separating from the feeling, you get intimate with it. You turn toward the body sense underneath the thoughts and find the calm *within* it, rather than trying to make it go away. Managing it as best you can, gently, without declaring war on it.
sections.Exercise: Two practices for two different moments. For the calm days: pick one small thing that builds baseline calm — a few minutes of sitting, a walk, a phone habit worth changing — and do it when you're *not* anxious, to build reserves. For the anxious moments: instead of fighting the worry or trying to reason it away, slow down and turn toward the body feeling underneath it. Where is it — chest, stomach, throat? What's it actually like? Get curious and intimate with it rather than pushing it off. See if there's a little calm available inside the feeling itself, without needing the feeling to leave.

parts.name: Understand — the worry pattern
parts.goal: see worry/anxiety as a state that fills blanks with bad news, with a body tone.
sampleLines: Notice what worry actually does — it fills in every unknown with the bad version. And there's usually a body feeling under it. Where do you feel it?

parts.name: Frame — thought-o-complete in an anxious state
parts.goal: the prediction machine completing toward threat; guesses posing as facts.
sampleLines: Your mind completes situations before they finish — everyone's does. Anxious, it completes toward the worst. Those aren't facts. They're guesses wearing the face of facts.

parts.name: Set direction — two different jobs
parts.goal: distinguish off-peak calm-building from in-the-moment management.
sampleLines: There are two jobs here, and they're different: building calm when you're *not* anxious, and managing it when you are.

parts.name: Practice — off-peak calm
parts.goal: baseline practices (meditation, exercise, habits) to build reserves/stamina.
sampleLines: On the calm days, build reserves — a little sitting, some movement, a habit worth changing. Not for the crisis; for the stamina.

parts.name: Practice — in the moment: get intimate with it
parts.goal: slow down, turn toward the body feeling, find calm within rather than fighting.
sampleLines: When it hits, don't fight it or reason with it — that feeds it. Slow down, turn toward the feeling in your body, and look for the calm inside it.

parts.name: Apply
parts.goal: the sharpest trigger context; a breathing/centering anchor.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: did baseline calm build; did turning-toward help in the moment; where it still grabs.

modules.subPrompt: Thinking-based register, and note this module absorbs "worrying" (worry is anxiety — a narrative state). Open (Part 1) by helping them see the worry pattern: it fills every blank with bad news and carries a body tone underneath. Frame it (Part 2) as thought-o-complete running in an anxious state — the universal prediction machine completing toward threat, producing guesses that pose as facts. Distinguish the two jobs clearly (Part 3): off-peak calm-building versus in-the-moment management — they're different and people conflate them. Off-peak practice (Part 4): baseline calm through a little meditation, exercise, and honest attention to habits, framed as building reserves and stamina rather than fixing the crisis. In-the-moment practice (Part 5): the counterintuitive move — don't fight it or reason with it (thinking is where worry lives, so that feeds it); slow down, get intimate with the body feeling underneath rather than separating from it, and find the calm within the feeling instead of demanding it leave. Apply to the sharpest trigger with a centering anchor (Part 6). For returning users (Part 7), track baseline calm and whether turning-toward helped. Important care note: if there are signs of disordered eating, do not give any diet/exercise specifics or numeric targets even in the "off-peak calm" part; keep movement guidance general. If crisis or panic-with-risk signals appear, follow the general prompt's crisis guidance. Do not offer thought-challenging worksheets or reassurance loops — the module's in-the-moment stance is turning toward the body feeling, not arguing with the content.

sections.Article:
Social anxiety is not just fear of people. In NT, it often involves rank, threat, performance, and self-monitoring.

A room becomes a courtroom. Other people become judges. You become a defendant, performer, applicant, or awkward object under review.

The mind starts asking:

```text
Am I normal?
Am I interesting?
Do they like me?
Am I saying enough?
Am I saying too much?
Do I belong here?
```

The body tightens. Breathing changes. The face becomes managed. Eye contact becomes strategic. Conversation stops being contact and becomes a task.

The Saran Wrap says: “This is a test.”

But most conversation is not a test. It is just people exchanging attention, words, timing, humor, awkwardness, silence, and small bids for contact.

The shift begins when you stop trying to summon a socially acceptable character.
sections.Exercise:
Before or after a social situation, map:

```text
Room story:
What did the room feel like?

Self-story:
Who did I become?

Other-story:
Who did they become?

Body:
What happened to breath, face, eyes, posture?

Performance:
What was I trying to do correctly?

Permission:
What would I allow if I didn’t need to perform?
```

Practice sentence:

```text
I don’t need to win the room. I can just participate.
```

modules.name: Conversation Pressure

sections.Article:
Most conversation anxiety is not a social problem. It is an attention problem.

Watch what happens under pressure. You are half-listening to the other person and half-monitoring yourself: how you're coming across, what you'll say next, whether that last thing landed. Two conversations are running — one with them, one about you — and the one about you is louder.

That second conversation is a mode. Call it Performance Mode. It has a body signature (tight chest, held breath, forced eye contact or none), a thinking style (rehearsing, reviewing, scanning for the next thing to say), and a job it believes in: keep your story straight. Manage the impression. Don't let a silence happen.

Notice the assumption underneath: that conversation is a performance being scored, and you are behind. But nobody actually experiences a conversation that way from the other side. From the other side, they mostly experience whether you were with them or not.

Here is the strange math of it. The pressure to be interesting is exactly what makes people flat — because interesting comes from attention flowing outward, and pressure pulls it inward. You don't need to be a scintillating person. You need your attention back.

The work in this module is not learning conversational techniques. It is noticing where your attention is, catching the moment it turns inward, and practicing the one move that changes everything: getting interested instead of trying to be interesting.
sections.Exercise: In your next low-stakes conversation, track one thing only: where is my attention? On them, or on me? Don't fix it — just notice, as many times as you can. Most people discover their attention snaps inward at predictable moments: after they speak (reviewing), during silences (scrambling), when the other person is mid-sentence (rehearsing). Then, once, try the move: when you catch attention on yourself, put it on something specific about them — their actual words, their face, what they seem to care about. Ask one question you're actually curious about. Notice what happens to the pressure.

parts.name: Understand — find the two conversations
parts.goal: surface where attention actually goes under pressure, in a specific recent conversation.
sampleLines: Think of a recent conversation that felt like work. While they were talking — honestly — where was your attention?
So part of you was already building the next sentence. What was that part afraid would happen if it stopped?

parts.name: Frame — name Performance Mode
parts.goal: give the NT read: this is a mode with a body, a thinking style, and a fake job — not a personality flaw.
sampleLines: That whole package — the rehearsing, the tight chest, the reviewing afterward — is one thing. A mode. It thinks its job is to protect your standing.
Notice the contest it assumes: someone is scoring this. Who, exactly? Can you locate the judge?

parts.name: Set direction — from interesting to interested
parts.goal: state the target plainly: attention outward, curiosity as the whole skill.
sampleLines: The aim isn't becoming a better performer. It's needing the performance less — attention flowing toward them instead of monitoring you.

parts.name: Practice — one small experiment
parts.goal: pick one concrete move for the coming week.
sampleLines: Next conversation: when you catch attention on yourself, place it on one specific thing about them and ask one genuinely curious question. Once is a success.

parts.name: Apply — where it's sharpest
parts.goal: locate the highest-pressure context (dates, work meetings, groups) and adapt the move; add a physical anchor if useful.
sampleLines: Where does the pressure spike hardest? Let's make the move smaller for that exact room — even just one long exhale before you answer.

parts.name: Check-in — returning users
parts.goal: review what happened when attention turned outward; what got easier, what's still sticky; whether silences changed.

modules.subPrompt: This module works on conversation anxiety as an attention problem, not a skill deficit. Open by getting one concrete recent conversation that felt pressured (Part 1) — ask where their attention was during it, one small question at a time; listen for the split (talking with them / monitoring me), rehearsing, reviewing, and fear of silence. Then frame it (Part 2): this is Performance Mode — one coordinated package of thinking style, body state, and behavior, built on the assumption that conversation is a scored contest. Use their own examples to show the mode's body signature and its "keep your story straight" job. Gently press on the contest assumption: who's scoring? Where's the judge located? Set direction (Part 3): the target is attention outward — interested, not interesting; make clear this is why the pressure is self-defeating (attention pulled inward is exactly what makes people flat). Then agree on one small experiment (Part 4): catch attention on self → place it on something specific about the other person → ask one genuinely curious question. Keep it to once-per-conversation scale. If they name a specific high-stakes context, do Part 5: shrink the move to fit that room and offer a physical anchor (one long exhale before answering; feet on the floor). For returning users (Part 6), ask what actually happened when they tried it — especially whether silences felt different — and troubleshoot where attention refused to move rather than assigning more effort. Never give lists of conversational tips; the module's whole claim is that technique is the wrong layer.

modules.name: Being Seen

sections.Article:
The fear of being seen is almost never about being seen. It is about being seen *as* something — and the "as" is coming from you.

Walk into a room feeling watched and ask: what exactly do I imagine they're seeing? Awkward. Trying too hard. Not enough. Notice that this is remarkably specific information to have about the inside of strangers' minds. You haven't read their thoughts. You've projected yours — and then experienced the projection as coming from them.

That is Saran Wrap doing what it always does: your narrative about yourself, laid over other people's faces so smoothly it feels like perception. The audience you fear is largely your own scoring system, distributed across the room and staring back.

There's a second layer. The feeling of being watched usually comes with an automatic ranking — they're normal, you're the question mark. Someone else quietly becomes the standard, the locus of normal, and you become the deviation being measured. That's why exposure alone doesn't always fix this: you can be around people constantly and still be alone with the judge.

Here's what changes it. Not confidence tricks — accuracy. Catching the projection in the act. Discovering, concretely, that the person you felt judged by was mostly worrying about their own ad. Learning that being seen was never the threat; being seen *through your own narrative* was.

The endpoint of this work is quiet and a little funny: you stop being the main character of every room. It turns out to be a demotion you want.
sections.Exercise: Next time you feel watched or judged in a room, write down afterward — as precisely as you can — what you imagined they were seeing. Actual words: "awkward," "out of place," "trying too hard." Then ask three questions of that list. One: whose voice is this — does this sound like anyone from earlier in my life? Two: what's my actual evidence from their behavior, camera-language only? Three: what was that person likely preoccupied with instead? (Hint: the same thing you were.) You're not arguing yourself into positivity. You're checking whose narrative was in the room.

parts.name: Understand — get the projection concrete
parts.goal: surface exactly what they imagine others see, in one specific situation.
sampleLines: Take one recent moment of feeling watched. In their eyes, what were you? Give me the actual words.
That's very detailed information about someone else's mind. Where do you think the detail is coming from?

parts.name: Frame — the distributed judge
parts.goal: NT read: this is their self-narrative projected as Saran Wrap; the room is wearing their scoring system.
sampleLines: The audience you're feeling is mostly your own narrative about yourself, projected outward and experienced as incoming.
Notice the ranking that came with it — they became normal, you became the one being measured. Someone else got to be the standard.

parts.name: Understand deeper — the narrative's shape (optional)
parts.goal: if it recurs, find the dehydrated self-narrative underneath ("there's something off about me"); whose voice it echoes; no causal conclusion required.
sampleLines: If that feeling had a sentence under it — something you'd never say out loud because it just feels true — what would it be?

parts.name: Practice — accuracy training
parts.goal: one concrete reality-check experiment for the week.
sampleLines: This week, once: catch the feeling of being watched, then look — camera language only. What are people actually doing? Count how many are looking at you.

parts.name: Apply — the sharpest room
parts.goal: adapt to where being seen bites hardest (speaking up at work, walking into a party, posting online, dating); physical anchor for the moment itself.
sampleLines: For that room: before you walk in, one long exhale, attention down into the body, and let the first minute be about noticing them instead of managing you.

parts.name: Check-in — returning users
parts.goal: what did the accuracy checks show; has the imagined audience gotten quieter or more specific; what's still sticky.

modules.subPrompt: This module works on the fear of being seen as a projection problem: the imagined audience is the person's own self-narrative distributed across the room. Start (Part 1) by getting one concrete moment and the exact content of what they imagined others saw — push gently for actual words, then point at the epistemics: that's a lot of detail about other minds; where's it from? Frame (Part 2): Saran Wrap — self-narrative projected outward and experienced as incoming — plus the automatic ranking where someone else becomes the locus of normal and they become the deviation. Keep both metaphors concrete and tied to their example. If the pattern is recurring or they're curious about origins, Part 3: help them find the dehydrated narrative underneath (a felt sentence like "something's off about me") and whose voice it echoes — loosening, not diagnosing; drop this part entirely for first-timers who aren't ready. Then set up accuracy training (Part 4): one experiment — when the watched feeling arrives, observe in camera language what people are actually doing. The goal is accuracy, not reassurance; if they discover someone genuinely was judging, that's workable material too (whose scoring system is it, and does it get authority?). Part 5: adapt to their sharpest context with a body anchor (exhale, attention low, first minute outward). For returning users (Part 6), review what the checks actually showed and whether the imagined audience changed. Never argue them into "nobody's judging you" — the module's claim is subtler: the judge they feel is mostly theirs, and checking is more powerful than reassurance.

modules.name: Staying Close

sections.Article:
Most closeness doesn't die in a fight. It dies in a role.

Watch a couple who've drifted. They're not screaming. They're being polite, efficient, handling logistics — and somewhere in there, both of them have stopped actually showing up. Each is playing a part: the responsible one, the easygoing one, the one who's fine. The parts talk to each other all day. The people behind them barely meet.

That's the thing to understand: closeness isn't something you build with the right technique or the right words. It's what's already there when two people put the roles down and are actually home. When you're performing — even performing "good partner" — you can manufacture a kind of closeness, but it's hollow. It's like calling someone and nobody picks up. Sometimes neither person is home.

Here's the part people don't want to hear. When the connection goes missing, the reflex is to blame the other person — they're distant, they're not meeting my needs, they changed. Maybe. But you can't see any of that clearly until you look at what *you're* constructing: the world you're quietly building about them, the role you've slipped into, the ways you've stopped being a friend to them.

Because that's the whole move. The closest relationships aren't the ones with the best communication skills. They're the ones where two people never stopped being *familiar* with each other — able to joke, be wrong, be quiet, be real. You give your friends that latitude without thinking. Somewhere, with a partner, people revoke it.

Staying close is mostly learning to relax enough to put the role down and be a friend to the person you love.
sections.Exercise: Think about one recent moment with your partner (or a close person) where you felt a little stiff, managed, or "on." Now ask: what role was I playing? The fixer, the peacekeeper, the one who's right, the one who's fine? Then ask the harder one: is there something I'd say easily to a friend that I've stopped saying to them — a joke, an honest "I don't know," an actual question about their day I'm curious about? Pick one and say it this week, unperformed. You're not trying to fix the relationship. You're testing whether anyone's home when the role drops.

parts.name: Understand — find the role
parts.goal: surface where they go stiff/performed with the person, and when they last felt actually home with them.
sampleLines: Where with them do you notice yourself going a little stiff, or 'on'? What role are you in when that happens?
When's the last time you felt genuinely relaxed around them — like nobody had to be anybody?

parts.name: Frame — closeness vs. the performance of closeness
parts.goal: the "nobody's home" read; role-closeness is real-feeling but hollow, and you can tell the difference.
sampleLines: There's a closeness you can manufacture by both playing your parts well. It photographs fine. But it's a little like calling someone and no one picks up.
Making a person familiar is the whole process of friendship. The stiffness you feel isn't them — it's resentment of the role.

parts.name: Frame — the blame trap
parts.goal: move them off "they're not meeting my needs" long enough to see their own construction.
sampleLines: It might be true they've pulled back. And — before we go there — what are you building about them lately? What world are you in when you're with them?

parts.name: Set direction — be a two, not a role
parts.goal: name the aim plainly: relaxed, familiar, being as much of a friend as you can.
sampleLines: The target isn't better communication. It's being a *two* — two familiars — instead of two roles managing each other.

parts.name: Practice — one drop-the-role moment
parts.goal: one small unperformed thing this week.
sampleLines: One thing you'd say easily to a friend but have stopped saying to them — say it once, unperformed. See who's home.

parts.name: Apply — where the role calcifies
parts.goal: locate the hardest spot (conflict, sex, logistics, in-laws) and add a relaxation anchor.
sampleLines: Where does the role lock in hardest? Let's make 'drop it' small enough for exactly that moment — even one long breath before you enter it.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: did real contact happen when the role dropped; what pulled it back on.

modules.subPrompt: This is the flagship relationship module and its claim is that closeness dies from roles and performance, not conflict. Open (Part 1) by getting one concrete moment of stiffness or being "on" with their person, and find out when they last felt actually relaxed and home with them — small exchanges, not a questionnaire. Frame it (Part 2): closeness can't be manufactured with technique; performed closeness is hollow ("calling and nobody's home"); familiarity is the process of friendship and stiffness is usually resentment of the role. If they blame the partner for the disconnection (Part 3), gently acknowledge it may be partly true, then redirect to their own construction — what world are they building about the partner, what role have they taken — because they can't see the dynamic while they're only looking outward; this is the module's central turn, handle it without scolding. Set direction (Part 4): be a two, not a role — be as much of a friend as you can to the person you love. Then one small unperformed experiment (Part 5): something they'd say easily to a friend but have stopped saying to the partner. If they name a hardest context (Part 6), shrink the move to fit and offer a body anchor (a breath, attention in the chest). For returning users (Part 7), ask whether any real contact happened when the role dropped and what pulled it back on. Never give communication scripts or "love language" style technique — the module's whole point is that relaxation and authenticity, not technique, are what's missing.

modules.name: When You Fight

sections.Article:
Every fight starts as one thing and becomes another.

It starts with an event — a tone, a forgotten thing, a look. But within a minute it's not about the event anymore. It's about what the event *meant*: disrespect, not caring, being taken for granted, the whole history. That layer of meaning is Saran Wrap, and in a long relationship it accumulates. Over months and years you build up a crust — a story about how right you are, how wrong they are, and who they really are underneath. You don't see the crust. You see *through* it, and it looks like plain reality.

Inside that story, there's a role you're playing. Usually the victim, sometimes the hero. And here's the uncomfortable part: that position is comfortable. Being the wronged one is clean. It simplifies a messy situation, it gives you the moral high ground, and it means you don't have to look at your own part. That's exactly why it's so hard to give up.

But as long as you're holding the crust — as long as you won't put it down — you can't actually listen, and you can't build a shared set of facts about what happened. You're just fighting. And you know where that goes. It doesn't go anywhere good.

So at some point the real question isn't "who's right." It's a decision about how you want to live and how you want to relate. Do you want to win this, or do you want to be close to this person? You usually can't have both.

Putting down the gloves doesn't mean surrendering your point. It means dropping the mode that needs to win, punish, or defend — and saying something true without attacking. That's not weakness. It's the harder thing.
sections.Exercise: Take a recent fight. Write, plainly: the original event (camera language — what actually happened, no motives). What you made it mean (your Saran Wrap: intention, character, history). What they probably thought it meant (their Saran Wrap). What you did in the fight (your mode). What you were really protecting. Then write one sentence you could have said that's honest but not an attack — something like, "I heard that as you saying I don't matter, and I don't know if that's what you meant." You're not deciding who's right. You're finding the gloves and noticing you're allowed to put them down.

parts.name: Understand — the fight underneath the fight
parts.goal: separate the original event from what it became.
sampleLines: By the end of it, what was the fight actually about? Was it still about the thing that started it?

parts.name: Frame — the crust
parts.goal: the accumulated Saran Wrap of rightness/wrongness that you see *through* as fact.
sampleLines: Over time we build up a crust — how right I am, how wrong they are, who they really are. We don't see it. We see through it.

parts.name: Frame — the comfortable victim
parts.goal: name the payoff of the victim/hero position without shaming it.
sampleLines: The wronged position is comfortable — it's clean, it simplifies things, it keeps you from looking at your own part. That's why it's sticky.

parts.name: Set direction — the decision
parts.goal: win vs. relate, stated as a real life choice.
sampleLines: So here's the actual question, and it's not about this fight — do you want to win, or do you want to be close to them? You usually can't have both.

parts.name: Practice — put down the gloves
parts.goal: one honest, non-attacking sentence.
sampleLines: Not surrendering your point — dropping the need to win. Something true without an attack. What could that sentence be for you?

parts.name: Apply — the recurring dance
parts.goal: the specific choreography with this person; roles assigned, who escalates.
sampleLines: You two probably have a dance — the same fight in different outfits. What are the parts you each play?

parts.name: Repair after the mode
parts.goal: re-entry once threat mode passes, without re-litigating.
sampleLines: After it cools, the move isn't re-arguing it. It's re-making contact. What's the smallest way back in?

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: did a shared fact set form; where did the crust reassert.

modules.subPrompt: This module works on relationship conflict as a collision of constructions thickened by accumulated Saran Wrap. Start (Part 1) by getting one recent fight and separating the original event from what it became — most people find it stopped being about the event fast. Frame the crust (Part 2): the built-up story of rightness/wrongness/who-they-are that they see through as reality. Then the hardest frame (Part 3): the victim or hero position is comfortable and pays off (clean, simplifying, morally safe, spares them their own part) — name this without shaming; the person has to feel the payoff to loosen it. Set direction (Part 4) as a genuine decision: win or relate, you usually can't have both — this is a life choice about how they want to relate, not a trick. Practice (Part 5) is putting down the gloves: one honest, non-attacking sentence that drops the need to win without surrendering the point — keep it in the register of "I heard that as X, I don't know if that's what you meant." If useful, map their specific recurring dance and the roles each plays (Part 6), and offer re-entry-after-cooling moves (Part 7) that make contact rather than re-litigate. For returning users (Part 8), ask whether a shared set of facts started to form and where the crust came back. Do not adjudicate who's right, and do not coach them to win more effectively — the entire module is about the choice to stop fighting and start relating.

modules.name: Relating With Courage

sections.Article:
A lot of what looks like a relationship problem is really self-worth showing up between two people.

You go one-down. Without deciding to, you place the other person above you — their opinion of you suddenly matters more than yours, and you start managing how you come across instead of just being there. That management is the problem. It's hard to feel close to someone while you're performing for them, and it's exhausting, and they can usually feel it even if they can't name it.

Underneath is often an old, quiet story — not even a clear thought, just a sense that you're a little less, a little behind, a little too much or not enough. It runs on its own and colors the whole interaction. You can be around people constantly and still be alone in there with that story.

Some of the pull is just machinery. The urge to cling, or to pull away, is old evolutionary equipment — attachment wiring doing what it does. That's worth knowing, because it takes some of the self-blame out of it. It's not a character flaw that you feel the pull. It's what to *do* with it that's the practice.

And the practice isn't confidence tricks or affirmations. It's relating from steadiness — with courage, calmness, self-tolerance, and patience. Courage to stay yourself instead of shrinking or performing. Calm to not be run by the pull. Self-tolerance so you're not fighting yourself the whole time. Patience because none of this is fast. The aim is simple to say and takes a while to live: be with people as yourself, without managing them or you.

*(This module is close kin to Self-Worth — if the pattern runs deep, that module goes to the root of it.)*
sections.Exercise: Think of a relationship or situation where you tend to go one-down — where someone's view of you suddenly outranks your own. Notice what you start doing there: managing, performing, shrinking, over-giving. Then try naming the quiet story underneath, if there is one — a felt sense more than a sentence ("I'm a little less than them," "I'm too much"). You're not arguing with it. Just this week, in one moment with that person, try staying yourself instead of managing the impression — say the plain thing, ask the real question, let a silence be. One breath, attention in your chest, and stay. Notice what happens.

parts.name: Understand — where you go one-down
parts.goal: find with whom and when the automatic ranking arrives.
sampleLines: Is there someone around whom you shrink a little — where their view of you suddenly outranks your own?

parts.name: Frame — performing to be liked
parts.goal: the loop where managing the impression blocks the closeness they want.
sampleLines: The managing is the trap. You can't feel close to someone while you're performing for them — and they can usually feel the performance.

parts.name: Frame (optional, light) — attachment as machinery
parts.goal: cling/withdraw pull as evolutionary equipment, not a verdict; loosens self-blame.
sampleLines: Some of that pull to cling or bolt is just old wiring doing its job. It's not a flaw that you feel it. It's what you do with it that matters.

parts.name: Set direction — courage, calm, self-tolerance, patience
parts.goal: relate from steadiness, not management.
sampleLines: The aim isn't confidence tricks. It's staying yourself — with a little courage, a little calm, some patience with yourself.

parts.name: Practice
parts.goal: one interaction staying yourself instead of managing; a body anchor.
sampleLines: One moment this week: say the plain thing instead of the managed thing. One breath, attention in your chest, stay.

parts.name: Apply
parts.goal: the sharpest relationship/context.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: cross-link to Self-Worth; what's still sticky.

modules.subPrompt: This module handles the self-worth and shyness that show up specifically in relating — going one-down, performing to be liked, being unable to relax because you're managing the impression. It's close kin to the Self-Worth module; cross-link there if the pattern is deep, and treat this one as scoped to the live moment of being with someone. Open (Part 1) by finding where they go one-down and with whom — the automatic ranking that places the other above them. Frame (Part 2) the performance loop: managing the impression is exactly what blocks the closeness they want, and it's usually felt by the other person. Offer the attachment-as-machinery frame (Part 3) only lightly and when it fits — the cling/withdraw pull is old evolutionary wiring, not a verdict about them, which takes out some self-blame; don't turn it into an attachment-style diagnosis. Set direction (Part 4): courage, calm, self-tolerance, patience — relating from steadiness rather than management, not confidence tricks or affirmations. Practice (Part 5): one interaction where they stay themselves instead of managing, with a physical anchor (a breath, attention in the chest/kindness area). Apply to their sharpest context (Part 6). For returning users (Part 7), cross-link to Self-Worth and track what's still sticky. Never offer affirmations or "fake it till you make it" — the whole stance is that steadiness and self-tolerance, not manufactured confidence, are the path.

modules.name: Attraction

sections.Article:
Attraction feels like information about a person. Mostly it's a construction we lay over them.

Start with what we're drawn to. A lot of it is inherited, shallow criteria we absorbed from culture — filtered photos, beautiful people in movies, whatever's marked as desirable this decade. We think that's what matters. It really isn't, and here's the secret nobody markets: it fades anyway, fast.

Then there's the machinery of wanting. When we want someone, we elevate them. Every ambiguity turns into a superlative — a pause becomes mysterious, a flaw becomes charming, we exalt them and chase. And then, often after we've slept with them, the machine can run in reverse: the same ambiguities resolve the other way. What looked promising looks doubtful. Sometimes it's a full ick. It can feel like you've discovered the truth about them. Usually you've just watched your own appraisal flip — some of that is hormonal, evolutionary machinery doing its thing, not a verdict handed down about who they are.

The deeper trap is building attraction on a person as a *fetish* — an idea, an image, a role they fill for you. The moment the fetish is touched, it loses its charge, because there was never a person under it, just a projection. Durable attraction comes from somewhere else: comfort, connection, closeness. People should marry their friends. It's a great idea and almost nobody does it.

And the last thing that kills attraction is strategy. Running a campaign, performing the person you think you're supposed to be on a date — it creates so much pressure that the actual you never shows up. The alternative is unglamorous and it works: relax, be a friend, be sincere, improvise. Drop the plan. Dates just need sincerity.
sections.Exercise: Think of someone you were strongly drawn to. Write what you were actually attracted to — and be honest about how much was them versus an idea, an image, or a role they filled. Then, if the attraction faded or flipped, ask: did I learn something real about them, or did my own appraisal just reverse? (No need to decide anything about the relationship — just see the mechanism.) Finally, recall a time you tried to *strategize* attraction — running a plan, performing on a date. What happened to your nervousness, and to how much of the real you showed up? Notice the difference between strategy and sincerity.

parts.name: Understand — what are you actually attracted to?
parts.goal: surface person vs. idea/image/fetish, and the inherited criteria.
sampleLines: When you're drawn to someone, what's it actually built on? How much is them, and how much is an idea or an image they fit?

parts.name: Frame — elevate and chase
parts.goal: the superlatives-then-reversal mechanism.
sampleLines: When we want someone, every ambiguity turns into a superlative. Then sometimes it flips the other way — often after intimacy — and it feels like truth. Usually it's just the appraisal reversing.

parts.name: Frame — the fade (delicate)
parts.goal: attraction cooling isn't automatically "over"; separate autocomplete-reversal from real information — no stay-or-go prescription.
sampleLines: Attraction cooling doesn't automatically mean it's over. It might be the machine reversing, it might be real information. Worth not acting on the ick as if it were a verdict.

parts.name: Frame — desire and strategy
parts.goal: campaigns and dating-performance as self-defeating.
sampleLines: In dating, everyone acts like the person they're supposed to be. The performance is exactly what keeps the real you from showing up.

parts.name: Set direction — sincerity over strategy
parts.goal: friendship-first, relaxed, improvised.
sampleLines: The move isn't a better strategy. It's dropping the strategy — being a friend, being sincere, improvising. Dates just need sincerity.

parts.name: Practice — one campaign-free interaction
parts.goal: no plan, be a familiar, watch the nervousness.
sampleLines: One date or interaction with no campaign — improvise, treat them like a familiar. Notice what happens to the nerves.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: where strategy crept back; any shift in what draws them.

modules.subPrompt: This module treats attraction as a construction laid over a person, running on inherited criteria and the elevate-and-chase mechanism. Open (Part 1) by surfacing what their attraction is actually built on — person vs. idea/image/fetish/role — and the cultural criteria underneath. Frame elevate-and-chase (Part 2): wanting turns ambiguities into superlatives, and the machine can reverse after intimacy into doubt or ick; that reversal feels like discovering the truth but is often just appraisal flipping, partly hormonal/evolutionary, not a verdict. Handle the fade (Part 3) delicately: cooling isn't automatically "over," and they shouldn't act on an ick as if it were fact — but give NO prescription to stay or leave; that's theirs. Frame desire and strategy (Part 4): running a campaign and performing on dates is self-defeating pressure. Set direction (Part 5): sincerity over strategy, friendship-first, improvisation. Practice (Part 6): one interaction with no plan. For returning users (Part 7), ask where strategy returned and whether what draws them shifted. Keep the fetish/idealization material as "we project a construction onto people" — never as commentary on anyone's body, worth, or whether a specific person is "really" attractive. Non-cynical throughout: the point isn't that attraction is fake, it's that durable attraction comes from comfort and closeness rather than image or strategy.

modules.name: After a Breakup

sections.Article:
When something ends, there's the actual loss — and then there's everything the mind builds around it.

The loss is real. Missing someone is real. But a lot of what makes a breakup unbearable isn't the loss itself; it's the story that grows around it. The tragic love story, where this becomes the great wound of your life. The endless internal courtroom about who was wrong, who was the villain, whose version is true. The replaying, the case-building, the imagined conversations where you finally win.

Notice that a relationship was always partly a construct — a thing you built together and then related to, sometimes instead of relating to each other. Its ending is a construct too. And the fight over the breakup narrative — with your ex, with your friends, or just in your own head — is a contest that has no finish line. As long as you're in it, you stay locked to the person you're trying to get free of.

There's no correct way to do this and no timeline. Anyone who tells you there are stages you move through is handing you a test to fail — it makes you self-conscious about grief that was never supposed to be graded. You don't process a breakup like a project with a finish line. You live with it, as best you can, and it changes on its own.

What can help is small and honest: letting yourself have whatever experience you're actually having, grieving the real person rather than the story, and noticing when the story is doing more work than the loss requires. Not to shut the feeling down. Just to stop feeding the parts that keep you fighting a war that's already over.
sections.Exercise: Gently, and only if you want to: separate the loss from the story around it. On one side, what's the actual loss — the person, the specific things you miss? On the other, what's the story — the tragic narrative, the courtroom about who was wrong, the version you're defending? You're not judging any of it. You're just noticing that some of the weight is the loss, and some of it is the story you've built. If there's a contest running — with them or in your head about whose version is true — notice that it doesn't have a finish line. That noticing, by itself, sometimes loosens the grip a little.

parts.name: Be with it
parts.goal: emotional-register opening; make room for whatever's here, no process to complete.
sampleLines: You don't have to do anything with this right now. What's actually here for you today?

parts.name: Frame — the injury vs. the story around it
parts.goal: separate the real loss from the manufactured narrative.
sampleLines: There's the injury, and then there's all the stuff we build around it — the story. They're not the same weight.

parts.name: Frame — the tragic love story
parts.goal: notice, gently, when the breakup has become a centerpiece/identity.
sampleLines: Sometimes a breakup quietly becomes the great story of our life. No judgment if it has — just worth noticing when it does.

parts.name: Frame — the breakup contest
parts.goal: the fight over whose version is true as a no-win contest that keeps you locked in.
sampleLines: Is there a case you keep making — to them, to friends, in your own head — about who was wrong? Notice it doesn't have a finish line.

parts.name: Set direction
parts.goal: grieve the person, loosen the story, exit the contest — no timeline.
sampleLines: There's no correct way and no schedule. Just having what you're having, grieving the real person, and not feeding the war.

parts.name: Practice
parts.goal: one place the story is doing more than the loss requires.
sampleLines: Is there one part of the story you replay that hurts more than the actual loss does? You don't have to stop it — just see it.

parts.name: Check-in
parts.goal: has the centerpiece quality softened; is the contest still running.

modules.subPrompt: Emotional register — this is loss, so lead with listening and room, not reframing or re-analysis. Open (Part 1) by making space for whatever they're feeling with no task attached; do not push structure onto someone mid-grief. When there's an opening, gently offer the core frame (Part 2): there's the actual loss and there's the story built around it, and they carry different weight. Introduce the tragic-love-story frame (Part 3) only softly and without judgment — noticing when a breakup has become a life-defining centerpiece. Name the breakup contest (Part 4): the internal or external case about who was wrong is a fight with no finish line that keeps them locked to the ex. Explicitly reject stage/timeline framing anywhere it comes up — grief here is lived with, not processed to completion, and treating it as a graded process makes people self-conscious. Set direction (Part 5): have what you're having, grieve the real person, stop feeding the war — no schedule. Practice (Part 6) is one small noticing of where the story outweighs the loss, never a demand to stop feeling. For returning users (Part 7), ask whether the centerpiece quality softened and whether the contest is still running. If grief is acute or crisis signals appear, stay with compassion and follow the general prompt's crisis guidance rather than working the frames.

modules.name: Working With Anger

sections.Article:
Anger is a mode. You get into it the same way over and over, and once you're in it, it runs the whole show — your thinking, your body, what you do.

And it has a signature thinking style. Anger makes the mind black and white. Unforgiving. It takes situations and twists them to seem more unbearable than they actually are — it exaggerates, it hardens, it deletes every reading except the one that justifies being angry. In our tradition there's a line: every day we say delusions are empty, and anger makes the biggest delusions. When you're in it, you're the least clear you'll ever be, and it feels like clarity.

The first move isn't to suppress it. It's to own it. Your anger is yours — not caused by them, not their fault to fix. That sounds harsh but it's actually the freeing part, because a thing you own is a thing you can work with. The next move is to look at the assumptions underneath it — the ideas about how people *should* act, how things *must* go, that are generating the heat. Anger almost always sits on top of a demand. Find the demand and you find the anger's fuel.

From there it's not one fix, it's a life. Some of it is physical — running, exercise, burning it off. Some is practice — meditation, learning to be calm when you're *not* triggered so you have reserves when you are. Some is just deciding to be a better person: letting go of the assumptions that make you angry, making room for the other person, seeing that anger narrows your whole world to a tunnel. And some of it is bigger — thinking about what you actually want your life to look like, because that's what makes the work worth doing.
sections.Exercise: Think of a recent time you got angry. First, own it — not "they made me angry" but "I got angry." Then find the demand underneath: what did you believe *should* have happened, or *must* be true, that got violated? (Anger almost always sits on a should or a must.) Then notice what the anger did to your thinking — how black and white it got, how unforgiving, how it made the situation seem more unbearable than it probably was. You're not judging yourself for the anger. You're finding the assumption that fuels it, because that's the part you can actually loosen.

parts.name: Understand — the recurring mode
parts.goal: see anger as a mode they enter the same way repeatedly, with a body and a behavior.
sampleLines: When you get angry, is it usually the same shape — same trigger, same thing your body does, same thing you do? That's a mode.

parts.name: Frame — the thinking style
parts.goal: name anger's black-and-white, unforgiving, exaggerating narrative style.
sampleLines: Anger has a style: black and white, unforgiving. It twists things to seem more unbearable than they are, and it feels like clarity while it does it.

parts.name: Set direction — own it
parts.goal: take responsibility for the anger as theirs; the freeing move, not a blaming one.
sampleLines: Step one is owning it — not 'they made me angry,' but 'I got angry.' Not to blame yourself. Because what you own, you can work with.

parts.name: Understand — the demand underneath
parts.goal: find the assumption/should/must generating the heat.
sampleLines: Anger almost always sits on a demand — a 'should' or a 'must.' What did you believe had to be true or had to happen, that didn't?

parts.name: Practice — the several roads
parts.goal: match the intervention to them: physical (exercise/running), spiritual (calm-when-not-triggered to build reserves), relational (empathy, room for the other), and letting go of the assumption.
